Maladaptive Strategies.value: try hard not think about the trauma
Going out at night or being outside after dark
Any form of physical contact with others

Memory.value: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

vignette: The abduction had lasted seventy-two hours in a windowless basement where the air grew thick with mildew and a guard’s heavy boots echoed against concrete. Malik, then seventeen, had learned to hold his breath when the metal door creaked open, memorizing the rhythmic clatter of chains and the low commands that filled the dark. He had come to believe that survival depended on staying utterly invisible, a lesson that stuck long after the rescue team cut the lock. Now, at nineteen, he carried that hyper-vigilance into his role as a detective. Yet when the sun dipped below the horizon, the memory of that swallowed daylight returned with a violence that left him gasping on his couch. Those memories refused to cooperate with his mind. He knew exactly what had happened, yet when he tried to speak about it to his girlfriend, the words dissolved, leaving only a hollow ache in his throat. Instead of pictures, he would hear the guard’s muttered threats and the metallic scrape of the lock, sudden enough to make him drop his coffee mug. Other times, the past arrived carrying the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image at all; a wave of panic would crash over him during patrol, his heart hammering as if the walls were closing in once more. Because these intrusive recurrences struck without warning and carried such raw intensity, he had developed a rigid habit of trying hard not to think about the trauma, forcing himself into avoidance to keep the floodgates shut. He started avoiding going out at night, telling his squad he had early dates when the heavy click of his patrol car door locking each evening became a trigger that instantly pulled him back to the basement. At the precinct, he began avoiding being touched; a colleague’s hand on his shoulder to hand him a file sent a jolt of dread through him, and he stepped back, claiming a sudden sensitivity to the station’s wool uniforms. Over the following weeks and months, the pattern repeated itself. Every time a memory breached his conscious mind, he reached immediately for suppression, spending his shifts standing near the perimeter of the evidence room, keeping his gloves on and his elbows tucked. The more he worked to block the intrusions, the more frequently his mind breached the walls he built, pulling him further into the dark and away from contact. His detective work was complicated by his inability to handle the evidence bags that required direct gloved contact, and he could not sit close to his girlfriend during quiet evenings when her legs naturally brushed his. He had come to believe that letting his guard down meant being trapped again, so he maintained a rigid distance that left his partner wondering where the man she met had gone. Now, after three years of sleepless nights and mounting suspicion from his supervisor, Malik sat in the intake office, fingers knotted around his jacket hem. He was ready to finally speak, though he was terrified the words would never come, hoping instead that someone could help him untangle the past from the present without losing his mind in the process.
